newsitem.title: FRANCE: French worried Zaire breakdown could spread.
newsitem.headline: French worried Zaire breakdown could spread.

text.p: France said on Thursday it had no plans to intervene in Kinshasa for the time being but officials privately expressed fears that threatened anarchy in the sprawling African capital could spread outside Zaire.
The rebel forces of Laurent Kabila are within striking distance of Kinshasa after over-running most of Zaire in a seven-month conflict.

"If our troops positioned in Brazzaville had to intervene, it would be strictly limited to evacuating foreigners," French defence ministry spokesman Jacques Servent told reporters. Brazzaville is the capital of Congo, across the river from Kinshasa.

"But as things stand today, there is no intention or reason to intervene. If we had to, it would be in close coordination with the other countries (the United States, Britain, Belgium and Portugal) who also have troops on the spot," he said.

But other officials who spoke to Reuters said there was widespread concern among western powers that a breakdown in law and order in Kinshasa might spark trouble in, or with, nearby states like Angola, the Central African Republic or Congo.

The officials spoke after a South African-brokered peace effort failed, leading France's foreign ministry to express deep disappointment and question Kabila's motives for failing to meet President Mobutu Sese Seko.

Officials who declined to be identified said the United States, which Paris has long accused of backing Kabila, was now trying to slow his advance on Kinshasa to try to ensure an orderly handover of power.

"Anarchy is in no one's interest because it spreads. Our troops in the Central African Republic are already starting to disarm soldiers coming across that border from Zaire, including Rwandan Hutus," an official told Reuters.
France has long backed Mobutu, who during the Cold War was seen by the West as a bulwark against communism.

"Of course Mobutu is morally undefendable but the Americans now realise Kabila isn't a great democrat either, and Washington is trying to get him to slow down. But Kabila also has his own private American advisers who may be pushing him to speed ahead," the official said.

He confirmed press reports several weeks ago which said two of Kabila's U.S. advisers were killed during the rebel advance. Their bodies were recovered and handed to the United States by French special force commandos, whose presence in Zaire is not officially acknowledged by Paris.
He added that Mobutu's own foreign backers, mercenaries from Western Europe and Serbia, might end up being his last defenders and were now being helicoptered into the Kinshasa area.

"It risks being a very messy situation. If five million residents of Kinshasa, including the Mobutu presidential guard, set about looting the city, there's no doubt there will be dead foreign civilians.
"If it starts at night, getting them out will be a nightmare," the official said. "What will happen to the infrastructure of the city is also a great worry."
About 3,600 foreign troops are poised to intervene, including some 500 Frenchmen, officials said. More French troops were at hand in the Central African Republic and Gabon if required.
